title: GSBR: Geometric SupportBehavior Regularization for Online RL

paper.title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
paper.abstract:
Abstract Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies – typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets – capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy’s support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization ( GSBR ), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy’s support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy.
Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average
success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest
average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with
about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.
Project website and open-source code: https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .

sections.heading: 1  Introduction
sections.text: Online reinforcement learning (RL) can be costly when every interaction happens on a physical system, so practical methods often rely on a behavior prior that focuses exploration on plausible actions. In robotics, such priors are now available at scale: vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) learn diverse behaviors from large demonstration datasets ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) , but often lack the robustness and throughput required for reliable deployment ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . RL fine-tuning can close this gap by updating a policy that is regularized toward the pretrained base model. This raises a general question for RL: how should a behavior regularizer preserve the base policy’s guidance while giving the actor enough freedom to improve on it? Improving upon base policies typically has two requirements: mode selection and local refinement. Consider a scene with two objects and the task is to grasp a specified target. Foundation models trained on large-scale data often produce diverse behaviors - and such base policies might have two action modes, one to grasp each object. The actor should be updated to discard the mode that reaches for the wrong object; we call this mode selection . However, existing behavior constraints can hinder one of the requirements and restrict policy improvement. Action regression ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ; Park et al., 2025b ) and distribution-matching regularizers ( Li and Levine, 2026 ; Fang et al., 2025 ) tie the actor to the base policy’s full action distribution, penalizing the actor even for discarding poor modes (Figure 1 (a)). Support constraints ( Kumar et al., 2019 ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) remove this penalty and permit mode selection, but can be too restrictive and often exclude optimal actions outside the base policy’s support (Figure 1 (b)). Our key insight is to allow both mode selection and local refinement by introducing a geometric relaxation of the support constraint. We introduce Geometric Support Behavior Regularization ( GSBR ), an RL algorithm that estimates the support of the base policy using finite samples, and regularizes actions differently based on whether they are inside or outside the support. Actions inside the estimated support incur no penalty, allowing the actor to discard poor modes and concentrate on better ones without preserving their relative frequencies. Outside the support, GSBR replaces the infinite penalty of a hard constraint with a finite one that grows with distance, reflecting that value estimates become less reliable far from the base policy. Because the support of a learned base policy is intractable to compute, we approximate it by the union of neighborhoods around actions sampled from the base policy, with a radius that adapts to the observed samples’ distances from each other. GSBR provides a practical sample-based geometric support regularizer fitting for the diverse distribution of large-scale robot foundation policies. Our contributions are (1) a geometric behavior regularizer that permits both mode selection and local refinement in RL finetuning, (2) a sample-based approximation of multi-modal action distribution with an adaptive radius, with error bounds and a guarantee that the error vanishes as the number of reference samples grows, (3) an evaluation across 19 tasks drawn from four benchmarks where GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Further analysis shows that our approximation closely matches the true support region and examines the effects of sample count and support radius.

sections.heading: Sample-efficient online RL.
sections.text: Learning from costly environment interaction is a central challenge in robotic RL. Off-policy actor–critic methods address this through experience reuse, high update-to-data ratios, and critic regularization to improve data efficiency ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Hiraoka et al., 2022 ) . Prior data and demonstrations can also help by initializing policies and values, supplementing replay buffer, and guiding exploration ( Ball et al., 2023 ; Nakamoto et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2023 ) . These algorithmic advances enable practical systems to learn contact-rich manipulation within hours of robot interaction ( Luo et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026a ) . GSBR is complementary to these advances : it further improves sample efficiency through a behavior regularizer that uses a frozen base policy as a prior, reducing unnecessary exploration while allowing policy improvement beyond the prior’s support.

sections.heading: RL with generative models, diffusion and flow policies.
sections.text: Diffusion and flow policies, including VLAs, represent multimodal behavior, but they require iterative action generation and complicate RL optimization. One family updates the generative model itself, through policy gradients, critic gradients, or denoising supervision ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Li and Levine, 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , or through distillation and advantage conditioning ( Park et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Mark et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Another keeps the model frozen and trains a lightweight actor that corrects its actions ( Silver et al., 2018 ; Johannink et al., 2019 ; Ankile et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , steers its latent noise ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) , or selects among sampled candidates ( Dong et al., 2026b ; Dong et al., 2026a ; Sun and Song, 2026 ) , sometimes distilling the result back into the base model ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2026 ) . GSBR is most similar to the second family; methods within it differ mainly in how the actor is tied to the base policy, which we compare next.

sections.heading: Behavior constraints for RL.
sections.text: Behavior constraints guide policy improvement using available experience or a pretrained policy, but differ in how they restrict mode selection and departures from prior behavior. Distribution matching and action regression. KL regularization penalizes reallocating probability toward higher-value modes ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Li and Levine, 2026 ) , and regression toward sampled actions favors their mean ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ; Tarasov et al., 2023 ) . FQL and RLT ( Park et al., 2025b ; Xu et al., 2026 ) alleviate this mode collapsing problem by explicitly conditioning on noise or reference-action, but their pairwise regularization still ties the actor to the modes of randomly drawn inputs. In contrast, GSBR allows the actor to focus on promising modes and drop poor behaviors (mode selection) without retaining a particular action pairing. Support constraints and approximations. Ideal support constraints allow the actor to choose freely among actions with non-negligible density under the behavior prior. They permit mode selection but block local refinement. BEAR, SPOT, and PRDC ( Kumar et al., 2019 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Ran et al., 2023 ) constrain the actor to dataset actions via sample-based MMD or a density estimator. However, they require access to the dataset and do not leverage a pretrained foundation model’s broader behavioral repertoire. DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) acts in the base policy’s latent-noise space, while best-of- N N methods select the highest-value action among sampled actions ( Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Both enable mode selection, but remain suboptimal when local refinement is needed. These limitations motivate GSBR , which constructs an unpenalized support region from the base policy distribution and applies a finite geometric penalty beyond it, allowing online exploration to depart from the prior’s support. Residual reinforcement learning. Residual policies allow local refinement, but are often bounded by a prescribed scale ( Silver et al., 2018 ; Johannink et al., 2019 ; Ankile et al., 2024 ) . BCQ, EXPO and EXPO-FT ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ; Dong et al., 2026b ; Dong et al., 2026a ) combine bounded corrections with value-based candidate selection to have both mode selection and local refinement. However, they only allow local refinement up to a fixed magnitude set as a hyperparameter, bounding the maximum allowed deviation without any guidance from the base policy. They can be interpreted as an implicit support constraint that admits an enlarged support region by a fixed radius . DICE-RL replaces the fixed magnitude by using a selectively dropped out squared-distance regularizer on the edit policy ( Sun and Song, 2026 ) . While this method can be viewed as an implicit support constraint with a geometric penalty for deviation, it creates constant optimization pressure that pulls even small edits towards each base policy sample. In contrast, GSBR explicitly approximates the support region for the base policy distribution, permitting in-distribution action to have zero behavior penalty, enabling free mode selection and refinement within the support region while allowing departures at a finite, distance-dependent cost.

sections.heading: Online RL with a pretrained behavior prior.
sections.text: In designing RL algorithms to interact with the MDP environment and optimize for the return, we leverage a behavior prior to guide exploration and training. We study online policy improvement with a frozen pretrained base policy π β \pi_{\beta} and an offline transition dataset 𝒟 off \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{off}} of task-specific transitions , e.g., demonstrations or base-policy rollouts. The learner collects additional experience through environment interaction and trains on both offline and online transitions. The base policy stays frozen and is accessed only through samples b ∼ π β ( ⋅ ∣ s ) b\sim\pi_{\beta}(\cdot\mid s) ; we require no access to its parameters or gradients, so π β \pi_{\beta} can be any generative model.

sections.heading: Challenges.
sections.text: Three properties make this setting difficult: (1) π β \pi_{\beta} is typically multimodal and its modes can differ widely in value, which behaviors are worth keeping depends on the task. (2) the base action support is intractable: we can draw samples but cannot enumerate all plausible actions (e.g., too expensive to enumerate for every state). (3) the critic is trained on limited data, its estimates are less reliable when the input is out-of-distribution; an actor that maximizes Q ϕ Q_{\phi} without restraint will exploit these errors.

sections.heading: 4  Geometric Support Behavior Regularizer (GSBR)

Section 4.2 approximates this penalty from base-policy samples and bounds the approximation error. Algorithm 1 describes the practical instantiation of our algorithm.

sections.heading: 5  Experimental Results
sections.text: In this section, we empirically evaluate the performance of GSBR against previous online RL methods that leverage a frozen base policy across benchmarks covering both state and pixel inputs with MLP and VLA base policies. Throughout our experiments, we answer the following questions: (1) Is GSBR an effective behavior regularizer for online RL, (2) how sensitive is GSBR to the choice of support radius and number of samples, and (3) how well does GSBR estimate the true support region?

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate all methods on 19 tasks across four benchmarks, each having different properties that may change the distribution of base policies. In RoboMimic ( Mandlekar et al., 2022 ) , we select four challenging tasks: can-mh , square-mh , transport-mh , and tool-hang-ph . Each task contains demonstrations collected by human operators of various proficiency levels and captures challenges like precise alignment and bimanual coordination. We test five variants of the cube-triple-task{1-5} in OGBench ( Park et al., 2025a ) . These long-horizon tasks contain a play-style exploration dataset that may lead to a base policy with many action modes and test the RL actor’s ability to drop bad actions while exploring better ones. The recently released benchmark OCBench ( Park and Levine, 2026 ) provides a more realistic dataset that emulates the statistical properties of human demonstrations. We select block-lite-double-task{1-2} and chamber-lite-easy-task{1-3} . In these three benchmarks, the base policy is an MLP behavior cloning policy trained on only the task-specific dataset, and both the base and RL policies receive state information from the simulator. To test each method on more realistic settings, we also experiment on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) with the fine-tuned π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -LIBERO base policy using pixel inputs. We hand-picked five tasks where the base VLA leaves room for improvement: task{14, 29, 54, 60, 64} . On these image-based tasks, the RL network trains a CNN from scratch. Since the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy is slow to sample from, we cache a set of reference actions and sample from these instead of sampling from the policy at each training step.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare GSBR with seven online RL baselines. TD3+BC ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ) trains a state-conditioned actor with a Q-maximization objective and a squared regression penalty to base policy samples. For expressive base policies, TD3+BC regularizes the action to the mean of the reference action distribution. RLT ( Xu et al., 2026 ) conditions a Gaussian chunk actor on a single sampled base policy chunk and penalizes deviation from that specific reference. While the conditioning alleviates the mode averaging problem, RLT cannot drop action modes. Residual Policy ( Silver et al., 2018 ; Johannink et al., 2019 ) scales and adds a learned correction to a sampled base policy action, so its deviation from the base policy proposal is limited. We follow the formulation of Dong et al. (2026a) and learn an action chunked residual policy conditioned on the base policy input. BFN ( Li et al., 2025 ) does not learn an explicit actor, instead formulating it as the base policy sample that maximizes the Q value. This is analogous to a hard support constraint since the implicit actor cannot generate actions outside the base policy’s support. DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) learns to steer the frozen base policy through its latent noise rather than directly producing corrected actions, also limiting the possible actions to the support of the base policy. We use the DSRL-NA variant for the state-based tasks and the DSRL-SAC variant for LIBERO. EXPO-FT ( Dong et al., 2026a ) combines bounded residual edit policy with best-of-N sampling at test-time to achieve mode selection. For a fair comparison, we freeze the base policy. DICE-RL ( Sun and Song, 2026 ) learns latent-conditioned residual corrections to base policy samples, applies selective BC regularization on the residual policy, and applies best-of-N sampling. All methods use the same offline data, online interaction budget, network size, and architecture. They also share training settings, including the action-chunk horizon, discount factor, and critic configuration. sections.heading: Is GSBR an effective behavior regularizer for online RL?
sections.text: GSBR demonstrates strong empirical performance across benchmarks compared to the baselines. As shown in Figure 4 and Table 1 , across 19 tasks, GSBR achieves 95% success rate and 0.95 normalized throughput, while the next-best baseline, RLT, achieves 92% success rate and 0.77 normalized throughput. On RoboMimic, while most methods have a similar success rate at around 95%, GSBR achieves the highest throughput, surpassing the next-best method, DSRL, by 20%. On OGBench, GSBR achieves a near-perfect success rate across all five tasks, which is about 9 percentage points higher in success rate and 33% (relative) higher throughput compared to RLT, the strongest baseline. On OCBench, most methods achieve a near-perfect success rate yet GSBR has approximately 13% higher throughput than TD3+BC. Further, we evaluate the performance of our behavior regularizer on LIBERO with a modern VLA as the base policy. Using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -LIBERO, the strongest baseline is DSRL in terms of throughput at 0.84 and RLT in terms of success rate at 86%. GSBR achieves 85 % 85\% success rate and 0.86 0.86 normalized throughput, closely matching or beating the best baselines on either metric. These results demonstrate that GSBR provides an effective behavior regularizer that empirically outperforms baselines in success rate and throughput, indicating that our regularizer allows the maximum deviation from the base policy while providing stabilizing guidance. sections.heading: How sensitive is GSBR to the choice of support radius and number of samples?
sections.text: We sweep over a range of N N , the number of base policy samples used to compute the behavior regularizer loss on cube-triple (Table 3 ) and find little effect on the performance of GSBR . The normalized throughput for N = 8 N=8 , N = 16 N=16 , and N = 32 N=32 is 1.0, 0.91, and 0.93, respectively. These results suggest that as few as eight samples from the base policy suffice for effective behavior regularization on these tasks. We also ablate the effect of computing the support radius r ℬ r_{\mathcal{B}} (Table 3 ). With r ℬ = 0 r_{\mathcal{B}}=0 , the throughput degrades significantly to only 0.66. This ablation supports the benefit of leaving neighborhoods around reference actions unpenalized, unlike in other prior works, allowing the actor to refine its actions within these neighborhoods without being pulled toward individual samples.

sections.heading: How well do we approximate the true support region?
sections.text: Figure 5 shows the empirical support of the base policy visualized on a bimodal state in cube-triple . We visualize the first two action dimensions using q = 0.9 q=0.9 , and the zero-penalty estimated support region C C is marked in golden bronze. We estimate the true support of the base policy with KDE cutoff at 95% from 5,000 base-policy samples. With only N = 3 N=3 references, the sampled actions cover one mode and miss the other. At N = 8 N=8 , the zero-penalty region already captures both modes while leaving the low-density gap between them penalized. As N N increases, the support radius shrinks as the local spacing between samples becomes tighter. On this particular state, the trained RL actor predicts an action slightly beyond the true support, which incurs little loss as it is close to the support region. sections.heading: 6  Conclusions
sections.text: Foundation models offer an appealing behavior prior for sample-efficient online RL, which raises the question of how to regularize an actor toward such a prior while still allowing it to improve. We introduce GSBR , a geometric support behavior regularizer that provides sufficient guidance without overconstraining policy improvement. We provide a theoretically motivated implementation that estimates the ideal loss using base policy samples. GSBR demonstrated strong empirical performance: Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the best prior method. One limitation of the method is that it uses multiple base policy samples at test-time, which may impose compute overhead and introduce more inference latency. Further, GSBR introduces an extra hyperparameter, the quantile q q , compared to other common methods. Although we tuned q q for the best performance, fortunately, Figure 7 shows reasonable performance across the full range of possible values. Validating GSBR on real robots is a natural next step. Future work could also explore alternative ways to construct the support radius that could improve performance or reduce hyperparameter count.

sections.heading: Buffer sampling ratio.
sections.text: We maintain separate offline and online replay buffers, 𝒟 off \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{off}} and 𝒟 on \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{on}} . Following the symmetric replay sampling strategy of RLPD ( Ball et al., 2023 ) , each training minibatch contains equal numbers of H H -step sequences from the two buffers. This retains access to prior experience as new interactions accumulate.

sections.heading: Rollouts and deployment.
sections.text: During a rollout, we sample reference chunks and obtain an action chunk from the actor without reference dropout. During deployment, we can optionally skip querying the base policy and run the actor with reference actions set to zero.

sections.heading: A.4  Training details
sections.text: We describe the shared training protocol for the state-based benchmarks, followed by method-specific settings and the configuration used for LIBERO. Unless specified otherwise, the state-based methods use the protocol below. Our training and evaluations were done on either A5000 GPUs or TPU V5E chips. Common training settings are described in Table 6 . We also report the hyperparameter sweep range and the selected values of each method in Table 7 and Table 8 . We select the hyperparameter value with priority on average success rate, and favor the configuration with higher average throughput if multiple runs have success rate within 2% of each other.

sections.heading: Base policies and datasets.
sections.text: For each training seed, we use a seed-matched flow-matching behavior cloning policy trained offline for 10 6 10^{6} training steps. The base policy produces action chunks and remains frozen during online RL. On RoboMimic and OGBench Cube Triple, it uses a four-layer MLP with 512 units per layer and 16 Euler integration steps. On the OCBench Block and Chamber tasks, it uses a residual MLP with four 1024-unit layers and 10 Euler integration steps. We clip sampled base-policy actions to the action bounds. For RoboMimic, we use the low-dimensional v1.5 datasets: multi-human (MH) demonstrations for Can, Square, and Transport, and proficient-human (PH) demonstrations for Tool Hang due to it not providing a MH dataset. For OGBench, we use the cube triple play dataset. For OCBench, we use the type 51 dataset shards and normalize each action dimension using its 1st and 99th percentiles.

sections.heading: Replay and online training.
sections.text: The RL components receive no offline pretraining. We initialize online replay with 50 episodes collected by the base policy, then train with minibatches of 256 sequences, split equally between the offline dataset and online replay. We use two gradient updates per environment step, except for the DICE-RL where we take the max performance between a UTD 2 and the effective UTD used for their results in robosuite. We do not filter transitions by success and use the environment rewards. RoboMimic supplies a binary success reward, and episodes terminate on success; Cube Triple uses the OGBench reward.

sections.heading: Tasks and observations.
sections.text: We evaluate on LIBERO-90 tasks 14, 29, 54, 60, and 64, with an episode limit of 400 environment steps and action chunks of length H = 10 H=10 . The frozen base policy is π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} with the pi05_libero configuration, which receives images from both cameras and proprioception. The RL actor and critic use CNNs with a 64 × 64 64\times 64 image and an eight-dimensional state as input.

sections.heading: Training and evaluation.
sections.text: LIBERO training uses online data only, without demonstrations. Base-policy reference chunks are cached and reused. Each unsuccessful chunk receives reward − 1 -1 , and a successful chunk receives reward 0 0 . The discount factor is 0.975 0.975 per chunk, and TD targets are not clipped. We train for 1,000 trajectories with 20 gradient updates per action chunk.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2611.05295v1 [cs.RO] 03 Nov 2026 GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL Charles Xu Jacob Berg Liyiming Ke Affiliation: UC Berkeley Physical Intelligence Sergey Levine Affiliation: UC Berkeley Physical Intelligence Abstract Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies – typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets – capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal. Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy’s support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization ( GSBR ), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy’s support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code: https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ . Figure 1: Left: (a) Behavior cloning regularizer matches the base policy distribution, not allowing the RL actor to drop poor modes. (b) Support constraint allows the actor to select the best behavior in the base policy distribution, but excludes improvements beyond it. (c) GSBR applies distance-based regularization on deviation outside the base policy support, allowing the actor to discard suboptimal behaviors and guide exploration beyond the prior. Right: GSBR achieves 23% higher normalized throughput across 19 tasks and 4 benchmarks than previous methods. 1 Introduction Online reinforcement learning (RL) can be costly when every interaction happens on a physical system, so practical methods often rely on a behavior prior that focuses exploration on plausible actions. In robotics, such priors are now available at scale: vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) learn diverse behaviors from large demonstration datasets ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) , but often lack the robustness and throughput required for reliable deployment ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . RL fine-tuning can close this gap by updating a policy that is regularized toward the pretrained base model. This raises a general question for RL: how should a behavior regularizer preserve the base policy’s guidance while giving the actor enough freedom to improve on it? Improving upon base policies typically has two requirements: mode selection and local refinement. Consider a scene with two objects and the task is to grasp a specified target. Foundation models trained on large-scale data often produce diverse behaviors - and such base policies might have two action modes, one to grasp each object. The actor should be updated to discard the mode that reaches for the wrong object; we call this mode selection . However, existing behavior constraints can hinder one of the requirements and restrict policy improvement. Action regression ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ; Park et al., 2025b ) and distribution-matching regularizers ( Li and Levine, 2026 ; Fang et al., 2025 ) tie the actor to the base policy’s full action distribution, penalizing the actor even for discarding poor modes (Figure 1 (a)). Support constraints ( Kumar et al., 2019 ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) remove this penalty and permit mode selection, but can be too restrictive and often exclude optimal actions outside the base policy’s support (Figure 1 (b)). Our key insight is to allow both mode selection and local refinement by introducing a geometric relaxation of the support constraint. We introduce Geometric Support Behavior Regularization ( GSBR ), an RL algorithm that estimates the support of the base policy using finite samples, and regularizes actions differently based on whether they are inside or outside the support. Actions inside the estimated support incur no penalty, allowing the actor to discard poor modes and concentrate on better ones without preserving their relative frequencies. Outside the support, GSBR replaces the infinite penalty of a hard constraint with a finite one that grows with distance, reflecting that value estimates become less reliable far from the base policy. Because the support of a learned base policy is intractable to compute, we approximate it by the union of neighborhoods around actions sampled from the base policy, with a radius that adapts to the observed samples’ distances from each other. GSBR provides a practical sample-based geometric support regularizer fitting for the diverse distribution of large-scale robot foundation policies. Our contributions are (1) a geometric behavior regularizer that permits both mode selection and local refinement in RL finetuning, (2) a sample-based approximation of multi-modal action distribution with an adaptive radius, with error bounds and a guarantee that the error vanishes as the number of reference samples grows, (3) an evaluation across 19 tasks drawn from four benchmarks where GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Further analysis shows that our approximation closely matches the true support region and examines the effects of sample count and support radius. 2 Related Work Sample-efficient online RL. Learning from costly environment interaction is a central challenge in robotic RL. Off-policy actor–critic methods address this through experience reuse, high update-to-data ratios, and critic regularization to improve data efficiency ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Hiraoka et al., 2022 ) . Prior data and demonstrations can also help by initializing policies and values, supplementing replay buffer, and guiding exploration ( Ball et al., 2023 ; Nakamoto et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2023 ) . These algorithmic advances enable practical systems to learn contact-rich manipulation within hours of robot interaction ( Luo et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026a ) . GSBR is complementary to these advances : it further improves sample efficiency through a behavior regularizer that uses a frozen base policy as a prior, reducing unnecessary exploration while allowing policy improvement beyond the prior’s support. RL with generative models, diffusion and flow policies. Diffusion and flow policies, including VLAs, represent multimodal behavior, but they require iterative action generation and complicate RL optimization. One family updates the generative model itself, through policy gradients, critic gradients, or denoising supervision ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Li and Levine, 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , or through distillation and advantage conditioning ( Park et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Mark et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Another keeps the model frozen and trains a lightweight actor that corrects its actions ( Silver et al., 2018 ; Johannink et al., 2019 ; Ankile et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , steers its latent noise ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) , or selects among sampled candidates ( Dong et al., 2026b ; Dong et al., 2026a ; Sun and Song, 2026 ) , sometimes distilling the result back into the base model ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2026 ) . GSBR is most similar to the second family; methods within it differ mainly in how the actor is tied to the base policy, which we compare next. Behavior constraints for RL. Behavior constraints guide policy improvement using available experience or a pretrained policy, but differ in how they restrict mode selection and departures from prior behavior. Distribution matching and action regression. KL regularization penalizes reallocating probability toward higher-value modes ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Li and Levine, 2026 ) , and regression toward sampled actions favors their mean ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ; Tarasov et al., 2023 ) . FQL and RLT ( Park et al., 2025b ; Xu et al., 2026 ) alleviate this mode collapsing problem by explicitly conditioning on noise or reference-action, but their pairwise regularization still ties the actor to the modes of randomly drawn inputs. In contrast, GSBR allows the actor to focus on promising modes and drop poor behaviors (mode selection) without retaining a particular action pairing. Support constraints and approximations. Ideal support constraints allow the actor to choose freely among actions with non-negligible density under the behavior prior. They permit mode selection but block local refinement. BEAR, SPOT, and PRDC ( Kumar et al., 2019 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Ran et al., 2023 ) constrain the actor to dataset actions via sample-based MMD or a density estimator. However, they require access to the dataset and do not leverage a pretrained foundation model’s broader behavioral repertoire. DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) acts in the base policy’s latent-noise space, while best-of- N N methods select the highest-value action among sampled actions ( Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ) . Both enable mode selection, but remain suboptimal when local refinement is needed. These limitations motivate GSBR , which constructs an unpenalized support region from the base policy distribution and applies a finite geometric penalty beyond it, allowing online exploration to depart from the prior’s support. Residual reinforcement learning. Residual policies allow local refinement, but are often bounded by a prescribed scale ( Silver et al., 2018 ; Johannink et al., 2019 ; Ankile et al., 2024 ) . BCQ, EXPO and EXPO-FT ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ; Dong et al., 2026b ; Dong et al., 2026a ) combine bounded corrections with value-based candidate selection to have both mode selection and local refinement. However, they only allow local refinement up to a fixed magnitude set as a hyperparameter, bounding the maximum allowed deviation without any guidance from the base policy. They can be interpreted as an implicit support constraint that admits an enlarged support region by a fixed radius . DICE-RL replaces the fixed magnitude by using a selectively dropped out squared-distance regularizer on the edit policy ( Sun and Song, 2026 ) . While this method can be viewed as an implicit support constraint with a geometric penalty for deviation, it creates constant optimization pressure that pulls even small edits towards each base policy sample. In contrast, GSBR explicitly approximates the support region for the base policy distribution, permitting in-distribution action to have zero behavior penalty, enabling free mode selection and refinement within the support region while allowing departures at a finite, distance-dependent cost. 3 Preliminaries Reinforcement learning. Throughout our experiments, we answer the following questions: (1) Is GSBR an effective behavior regularizer for online RL, (2) how sensitive is GSBR to the choice of support radius and number of samples, and (3) how well does GSBR estimate the true support region? 5.1 Experimental Setup Benchmarks. We evaluate all methods on 19 tasks across four benchmarks, each having different properties that may change the distribution of base policies. In RoboMimic ( Mandlekar et al., 2022 ) , we select four challenging tasks: can-mh , square-mh , transport-mh , and tool-hang-ph . Each task contains demonstrations collected by human operators of various proficiency levels and captures challenges like precise alignment and bimanual coordination. We test five variants of the cube-triple-task{1-5} in OGBench ( Park et al., 2025a ) . These long-horizon tasks contain a play-style exploration dataset that may lead to a base policy with many action modes and test the RL actor’s ability to drop bad actions while exploring better ones. The recently released benchmark OCBench ( Park and Levine, 2026 ) provides a more realistic dataset that emulates the statistical properties of human demonstrations. We select block-lite-double-task{1-2} and chamber-lite-easy-task{1-3} . In these three benchmarks, the base policy is an MLP behavior cloning policy trained on only the task-specific dataset, and both the base and RL policies receive state information from the simulator. To test each method on more realistic settings, we also experiment on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) with the fine-tuned π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -LIBERO base policy using pixel inputs. We hand-picked five tasks where the base VLA leaves room for improvement: task{14, 29, 54, 60, 64} . On these image-based tasks, the RL network trains a CNN from scratch. Since the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy is slow to sample from, we cache a set of reference actions and sample from these instead of sampling from the policy at each training step. Baselines. We compare GSBR with seven online RL baselines. TD3+BC ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ) trains a state-conditioned actor with a Q-maximization objective and a squared regression penalty to base policy samples. For expressive base policies, TD3+BC regularizes the action to the mean of the reference action distribution. RLT ( Xu et al., 2026 ) conditions a Gaussian chunk actor on a single sampled base policy chunk and penalizes deviation from that specific reference. While the conditioning alleviates the mode averaging problem, RLT cannot drop action modes. Residual Policy ( Silver et al., 2018 ; Johannink et al., 2019 ) scales and adds a learned correction to a sampled base policy action, so its deviation from the base policy proposal is limited. We follow the formulation of Dong et al. (2026a) and learn an action chunked residual policy conditioned on the base policy input. BFN ( Li et al., 2025 ) does not learn an explicit actor, instead formulating it as the base policy sample that maximizes the Q value. This is analogous to a hard support constraint since the implicit actor cannot generate actions outside the base policy’s support. DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) learns to steer the frozen base policy through its latent noise rather than directly producing corrected actions, also limiting the possible actions to the support of the base policy. We use the DSRL-NA variant for the state-based tasks and the DSRL-SAC variant for LIBERO. EXPO-FT ( Dong et al., 2026a ) combines bounded residual edit policy with best-of-N sampling at test-time to achieve mode selection. For a fair comparison, we freeze the base policy. DICE-RL ( Sun and Song, 2026 ) learns latent-conditioned residual corrections to base policy samples, applies selective BC regularization on the residual policy, and applies best-of-N sampling. All methods use the same offline data, online interaction budget, network size, and architecture. They also share training settings, including the action-chunk horizon, discount factor, and critic configuration. GSBR demonstrates strong empirical performance across benchmarks compared to the baselines. As shown in Figure 4 and Table 1 , across 19 tasks, GSBR achieves 95% success rate and 0.95 normalized throughput, while the next-best baseline, RLT, achieves 92% success rate and 0.77 normalized throughput. On RoboMimic, while most methods have a similar success rate at around 95%, GSBR achieves the highest throughput, surpassing the next-best method, DSRL, by 20%. On OGBench, GSBR achieves a near-perfect success rate across all five tasks, which is about 9 percentage points higher in success rate and 33% (relative) higher throughput compared to RLT, the strongest baseline. On OCBench, most methods achieve a near-perfect success rate yet GSBR has approximately 13% higher throughput than TD3+BC. Further, we evaluate the performance of our behavior regularizer on LIBERO with a modern VLA as the base policy. Using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -LIBERO, the strongest baseline is DSRL in terms of throughput at 0.84 and RLT in terms of success rate at 86%. GSBR achieves 85 % 85\% success rate and 0.86 0.86 normalized throughput, closely matching or beating the best baselines on either metric. These results demonstrate that GSBR provides an effective behavior regularizer that empirically outperforms baselines in success rate and throughput, indicating that our regularizer allows the maximum deviation from the base policy while providing stabilizing guidance. The RL actor learned an action just outside the support region (marked with star). 6 Conclusions Foundation models offer an appealing behavior prior for sample-efficient online RL, which raises the question of how to regularize an actor toward such a prior while still allowing it to improve. We introduce GSBR , a geometric support behavior regularizer that provides sufficient guidance without overconstraining policy improvement. We provide a theoretically motivated implementation that estimates the ideal loss using base policy samples. GSBR demonstrated strong empirical performance: Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the best prior method. One limitation of the method is that it uses multiple base policy samples at test-time, which may impose compute overhead and introduce more inference latency. Further, GSBR introduces an extra hyperparameter, the quantile q q , compared to other common methods. Although we tuned q q for the best performance, fortunately, Figure 7 shows reasonable performance across the full range of possible values. Validating GSBR on real robots is a natural next step. Future work could also explore alternative ways to construct the support radius that could improve performance or reduce hyperparameter count.
